questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Vector quantities and scalar quantities
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a vector quantity from a scalar quantity
questions.stem: A push of 40 newtons is applied to a crate from the east, and a crate on the other side is pulled 30 newtons toward the north. Which statement correctly separates what these two numbers describe?

options.text: Both are vector quantities, since a force needs a size and a direction to act
Both are scalar quantities, since a newton is a plain count of how hard it is
options.misconception: reads a newton as a bare count with no direction attached to it

options.text: The push is a vector but the pull is a scalar, since they point different ways
options.misconception: believes the same unit forces different kinds of quantity by direction alone

options.text: Both are scalars, since the two numbers can simply be added to get 70
options.misconception: adds two forces of different directions and treats the sum as a plain count

questions.explanation: A vector quantity is not fully described until both its size and its direction are given, and that is exactly the situation of a force, since a 40 newton push is a different physical situation from a 40 newton pull. A scalar, by contrast, is completely described by its number alone, so 30 newtons would be a scalar only if the direction were irrelevant, which for a force it never is. The two quantities here can be combined, but only into another vector, never into the plain number 70.
questions.hint: Ask whether two forces of the same size in different directions are the same situation.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Resultant of two vectors
questions.learningObjective: explain why the resultant of two vectors need not be the sum of their magnitudes
questions.stem: Two ropes of 100 units each pull a barge, one due east and the other due north. How long is the single pull that replaces both, and how does it compare with 200 units?

options.text: About 141 units, since the two pulls combine at a right angle
Exactly 200 units, since the rope lengths are simply added together
options.misconception: adds the two magnitudes as though the pulls were parallel and aligned

options.text: Exactly 100 units, since a right angle makes each pull cancel the other
options.misconception: believes perpendicular pulls annihilate one another like opposite forces

options.text: About 240 units, since pushing at an angle makes the pull slightly longer
options.misconception: guesses at an increase with no theorem to justify any gain at all

questions.explanation: The single pull that replaces two pulls is the diagonal of a rectangle whose sides are the two pulls themselves, so for pulls at right angles the length is the square root of 100 squared plus 100 squared, which is 100 times the square root of 2, about 141 units. The sum of the magnitudes, 200 units, is what the pull would be if the two ropes pointed the same way, and it is the largest possible combined pull. Any angle between the ropes gives something between 141 and 200 units, never more.
questions.hint: Draw the two pulls as sides of a rectangle and look at the diagonal.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: What the dot product measures
questions.learningObjective: interpret the dot product as a projection weighted by length
questions.stem: One road points east and another points north-east, and someone multiplies corresponding parts of the two direction lists and adds the products. What has that number measured?

options.text: The length of the first road's shadow along the second, scaled by its own length
The area of the rectangle built on the two roads, since parts were multiplied
options.misconception: confuses the dot product with the cross product's measure of area

options.text: The average of the two lengths, since a dot product takes a middle value
options.misconception: believes multiplying parts and adding must always produce a mean

options.text: The total turn from one road to the other, measured as a signed angle
options.misconception: reads a product of cosines as though it reported an angle directly

questions.explanation: The dot product of two vectors is the length of the first, times the length of the second, times the cosine of the angle between them, and grouping the first two factors shows it as that second length scaled by the projection of the first onto it. A cosine of one means the shadow is the whole second vector, a cosine of zero means the two are at right angles and cast no shadow at all, and a negative cosine means the shadow falls backwards. The area reading belongs to the cross product, whose sine factor measures the part perpendicular instead.
questions.hint: Rewrite the product as one length times a projection of the other.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: What the cross product measures
questions.learningObjective: interpret the magnitude of a cross product as an area
questions.stem: Two rods are hinged at a common end and stretched apart so that the angle between them is 30 degrees. What does the magnitude of their cross product measure here?

options.text: The area of the parallelogram built on the two rods, using the sine of the angle
The area of the triangle between the rods, using the sine of the angle
options.misconception: halves the parallelogram and reports the triangle that sits inside it

options.text: The length of the diagonal across the far ends of the two rods
options.misconception: confuses the area with the diagonal that closes the figure on the far side

options.text: The product of the two rod lengths, with the angle left out of it
options.misconception: drops the sine factor, which is the whole content of the cross product

questions.explanation: The magnitude of a cross product is one length times the other times the sine of the angle between them, and the area of a parallelogram with those side lengths and that included angle is exactly that product. The sine is the part of the second rod that stands perpendicular to the first, and a parallelogram is precisely the first rod swept along that perpendicular part. Halving gives the triangle, so the answer to the triangle is half of the cross product's magnitude, not the whole of it.
questions.hint: Sweep one rod along the part of the other that stands perpendicular to it.

questions.topic: Recognising perpendicular vectors
questions.learningObjective: recognise orthogonal vectors from a zero dot product
questions.stem: Two direction lists are compared and, after multiplying matching parts and adding, the result comes out as exactly zero. What has just been established about the two directions?

options.text: They are at right angles, since the cosine of the angle between them is zero
They are parallel, since a zero result is what equal directions produce
options.misconception: thinks a zero result means the directions coincide rather than cross

options.text: They are the same direction but of lengths that happen to cancel
options.misconception: believes cancelling lengths in opposite senses gives a zero dot product

options.text: They are opposite, since a negative product and a zero read alike
options.misconception: cannot tell a zero from a negative and so accepts two unrelated cases

questions.explanation: The dot product is one length times the other times the cosine of the angle between them, and the only angle whose cosine is zero is the right angle, so a zero dot product is exactly the test for orthogonality. A pair of parallel directions would give a positive result equal to the product of the lengths, and a pair of opposite directions would give the negative of that, never zero. That is what makes the zero result a clean and unmistakable signal.
questions.hint: Ask which single angle has a cosine of zero.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: What determines a plane in space
questions.learningObjective: state what data determines a plane in three dimensions
questions.stem: A flat sheet of steel must be positioned in a workshop. What is the least that has to be specified before the sheet's position is fixed in space?

options.text: Three points on it that do not all lie along one straight line
Two points on it, since any two points fix a line and the sheet is a line
options.misconception: thinks two points determine a whole flat sheet rather than only a line

options.text: One point and one length, since a point plus a size fixes a position
options.misconception: believes a size measurement can substitute for a second direction

options.text: Three points on it, with the three allowed to lie along one straight line
options.misconception: misses that three collinear points leave the sheet free to hinge about

questions.explanation: A plane has two directions of freedom inside it, and each point supplied removes one, so three points fix it provided they are not all on one line. If the three are collinear they determine only the single line through them, and a flat sheet containing that line could still hinge about it to any tilt, so the position is not fixed. Two points are worse still, since they leave a whole family of planes rotating about the line joining them.
questions.hint: Count how many directions of freedom a plane has, and how many each point removes.

questions.topic: Skew lines in space
questions.learningObjective: define skew lines and distinguish them from parallel lines
questions.stem: Two straight rails in a workshop neither meet at any point nor run in the same direction, and they cannot be made to meet by sliding one along its own length. How would a surveyor classify the pair?

options.text: Skew, since they lie in no single plane and share no point at all
Parallel, since they keep the same gap between them as they extend
options.misconception: carries the two-dimensional picture of parallel lines into three dimensions

options.text: Perpendicular, since no meeting point can be found anywhere along them
options.misconception: reads the absence of a meeting point as though it meant a right angle

options.text: Intersecting, since any two lines through space must share one point
options.misconception: assumes the two-dimensional fact that two lines must meet somewhere

questions.explanation: Two lines that lie in one plane either meet at a point or are parallel, so if a pair does neither then no single plane contains them both, and that is the definition of skew. In three dimensions this case is genuinely new, because two lines can pass close by forever without any plane holding them, which never happens in a flat drawing. The absence of a meeting point says nothing about angles, and a constant gap is a statement about parallel lines, not about skew ones.
questions.hint: Ask whether one flat sheet could be laid down so that both lines lie in it.

questions.topic: Cross-section of a cone parallel to its base
questions.learningObjective: describe a cross-section of a cone cut parallel to its base
questions.stem: A cone stands upright and a plane slices it horizontally, well above the base. What shape does the cut face have, and how does its size relate to the base?

options.text: A circle, and its radius shrinks in proportion to how high the cut is made
An ellipse, since the cutting plane meets the sloping sides at a slant
options.misconception: confuses a tilted cut of a cone with a cut parallel to its base

options.text: A circle of the same radius as the base, since every cross-section agrees
options.misconception: believes every cross-section of a solid is the same size as its base

options.text: A triangle, since the cone tapers and the cut copies that taper flat
options.misconception: copies the cone's taper and calls the flat cut a triangle

questions.explanation: A plane parallel to the base of a cone meets the circular base in a direction parallel to itself, and by the parallel-clone theorem the cut face is a circle similar to the base, with the linear scale set by how far up the cone the cut is made. questions.hint: Ask what shape a plane parallel to the base circle cuts, then how the taper scales it.

questions.learningObjective: describe a cross-section of a pyramid cut parallel to its base
questions.stem: A square pyramid stands on a base of 10 metres a side, and a plane slices it parallel to that base at half the perpendicular height. What does the cut face look like?

options.text: A square of 5 metres a side, since the linear scale is the same as the height scale
A square of 10 metres a side, since the cutting plane never changes the base
options.misconception: halves the area and then forgets that area scales as the square

options.text: A square whose area is half that of the base, which means 5 metres a side
options.misconception: believes a parallel cut leaves the base size completely unchanged

options.text: A square rotated away from the base by 45 degrees at the halfway height
options.misconception: mixes up a linear scale of one half with an area scale of one half

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Parametric description of a line in space
questions.learningObjective: interpret a parametric form of a line in three dimensions
questions.stem: A line in space is given as the starting point (2, 1, 4) plus a number t times the list (0, 0, 3), where t runs over all real numbers. What does this describe?

options.text: Every point reached by moving from (2, 1, 4) straight up or down parallel to z
Every point on the vertical line through the origin, since t scales all three parts
options.misconception: ignores the zeros and believes all three coordinates change with t

options.text: The single point (2, 1, 4), since a list of three numbers fixes one location
options.misconception: believes a one-number parameter can only describe a single point

options.text: A circle in the plane z equals 4, since t traces a round shape on its own
options.misconception: supposes a linear parameter traces a curve rather than a straight line

A direction with several nonzero entries would let the point travel in a slanted direction, and a quadratic rather than linear parameter would trace a curve instead.

questions.stem: Two direction lists are (1, 1) and (1, 0) on a flat grid. What is the cosine of the angle between them, to the nearest hundredth? Report the number only.

The dot product here is 1 times 1 plus 1 times 0, that is 1, the first magnitude is the square root of 2 and the second is 1, so the cosine is 1 over the square root of 2, that is 0.71. (0, 0, 0), since the two lists share a zero part and so cancel wholly
options.misconception: believes one shared zero part annihilates a cross product entirely

options.text: (1, 0, 0), which is the first list with its parts taken in reverse order

questions.topic: Why a cross product measures a parallelogram
questions.learningObjective: derive the area interpretation of a cross product's magnitude
questions.stem: Explain why the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors is the area of the parallelogram built on them, and identify the factor in that formula that a dot product does not have.

answer.exemplar: A parallelogram with two adjacent sides of lengths a and b meeting at an angle t has base a and height b times the sine of t, because the sine of t is the fraction of the second side that stands perpendicular to the first. Its area is therefore a times b times the sine of t. The magnitude of the cross product of two vectors is, by its own definition, the product of their two lengths times the sine of the angle between them, so it coincides with that area exactly. The factor the cross product carries and the dot product does not is the sine in place of the cosine. That single swap is the whole difference between the two products: the dot product keeps the part of the second vector lying along the first and measures projection, while the cross product keeps the part standing at right angles to the first and measures area. A triangle on the same two sides covers half of that parallelogram, so its area is half the cross product's magnitude.

questions.explanation: Both products share the same two lengths and differ only in which trigonometric function they carry, and that choice of function is exactly the choice of which part of one vector to keep. The parallelogram's height is the perpendicular component of the second side, which is where the sine comes from, so the cross product is an area and the dot product is a projection. Halving the cross product turns the parallelogram into the triangle that shares its two sides, which is the standard correction whenever a triangle's area is wanted.

Multiplying that area by the component of w perpendicular to the base plane gives the volume, and taking the dot product of u by v with w does exactly that multiplication, because the dot product multiplies a length by the component of the other along it. A right triangle in the plane of the two vectors gives the same reading, since the far corner of that triangle projects onto the path at the foot of the perpendicular. The part of v left over runs across the path and forms the other leg of that same triangle, so its length is the magnitude of v times the sine of the angle. The cosine therefore keeps the part that helps, and the sine keeps the part that does not, and the two squares add back to the whole square of the length. This is why a push at a right angle to the path does no work along it at all even though the push is perfectly real.

The leftover is the other leg of the same triangle, so it is a sine-weighted length, and the two pieces are related by the familiar identity that the squares of a sine and a cosine add to one. answer.exemplar: A point in space has three degrees of freedom, since each of its three coordinates can vary on its own. A point on a given plane has only two, because being on the plane is one restriction and it costs exactly one of the three. Each additional point of the plane therefore removes one further freedom: the first point leaves a two-dimensional family of planes through it, the second leaves a one-dimensional family, all the planes through the line joining the two points, and the third leaves none, provided it is not on that line. If the third point is on the line, then the family of planes through the line is untouched and the position is not fixed, which is why non-collinearity is the extra condition and not an afterthought. Two points leave a whole family of planes rotating about the line between them, and it is the third point that closes the family, but only if it lies off that line. One point and one direction describe a line instead, which is a useful reminder that the number of pieces of data has to match the number of freedoms being removed.

options.text: No single plane contains both of them, which is the definition of skew
The distance between them changes steadily as one slides along its own length
options.misconception: borrows the constant-gap property of parallel lines and applies it to skew ones

options.text: They lie in two different planes that share a line running beside both of them
The two lines can be made to meet by moving one along its own direction
options.misconception: believes sliding a line along itself can bring it into contact with a skew line

questions.explanation: Skew lines are defined by what no plane can contain, so the absence of a single common plane is the defining fact and is certainly true. A third line can always be found running beside both, so each of the two lines lies in a plane that shares that third line with the other, which is a useful picture of why the pair escapes every flat surface. A constant gap belongs to parallel lines, and sliding a line along itself does not change which plane it lies in, so neither of the last two statements can hold for a skew pair.
questions.hint: Start from the definition, then ask whether a third line can run beside both.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Matching the scale law to the quantity
questions.learningObjective: match the first, second and third power of a scale factor to the right quantity
questions.stem: A solid is enlarged so that every length is multiplied by a factor of 3. Which of the following quantities end up multiplied by 27?

options.text: The volume, which multiplies one length once for each of its three dimensions
The surface area, which multiplies one length for each of its two dimensions
options.misconception: gives a surface the third power because the solid was enlarged in three dimensions

options.text: The length of any edge, which is simply the factor used to begin with
options.misconception: confuses a length with a two-dimensional measurement and cubes it as well

options.text: The total length of a wire wrapped twice around the solid, one length factor

questions.explanation: The power that applies is the number of independent directions the measurement is built from. A volume is a product of three lengths, so it gains a factor of 27, and a wire wrapped around a solid is still a single length however many times it goes round, so it gains only the factor of 3. A surface area is a product of two lengths and gains 9, not 27, and an edge is a length and gains 3. The whole question reduces to counting the directions, and mixing up that count is the only real trap in it.
questions.hint: For each quantity, count how many independent lengths it multiplies together.

options.misconception: uses the block's width as the length of the hole through it

questions.topic: Classifying two lines given by points and directions
questions.learningObjective: classify two lines in space as parallel, intersecting or skew
questions.stem: A first line in a workshop passes through (0, 0, 0) with direction list (1, 0, 0). A second line passes through (0, 0, 1) with direction list (0, 1, 0), all values in metres. How do the two lines stand in relation to one another?

options.text: Skew, since their directions differ and the second line misses the first entirely
Parallel, since the second line stays one metre above the first for ever
options.misconception: reads a constant vertical gap as though it made the lines parallel

options.text: Intersecting, since the second line's start lies directly above the first line
options.misconception: treats lying above a line as though it meant meeting it at a point

options.text: Perpendicular, since the two direction lists share an entry of zero
options.misconception: reads a shared zero entry as a sign of a right angle between the lines

questions.explanation: The two directions (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0) are not parallel, since one runs along the first axis and the other along the second. Could they meet? Every point of the first line has second and third coordinates zero, while the second line's points have second coordinate free but third coordinate always 1, so no point of the first line is ever on the second. Since the directions are not parallel and no common point exists, the lines are skew, and no single plane contains them both.
questions.hint: Test for parallel directions first, then test whether any single point lies on both.

questions.topic: Volume of a tetrahedron from three edges at a corner
questions.learningObjective: find the volume of a tetrahedron from three mutually perpendicular edges
questions.stem: A tetrahedral steel block has three edges of 2, 3 and 4 metres meeting at right angles at one corner, each edge running along a different axis. What is the volume of the block in cubic metres?

options.text: 4, a sixth of the box built on the same three edges
24, which is the volume of the whole box and ignores the sloping face
options.misconception: reports the enclosing box rather than the solid with the sloping face

options.text: 12, which halves the box on the assumption of a flat bottom face
options.misconception: halves a box when a tetrahedron is a sixth of it, not a half

options.text: 8, which is the third power of the base edge and forgets the height
options.misconception: cubes a single edge and lets the perpendicular height out of the answer

questions.explanation: The three edges are mutually perpendicular, so they are the three edge lengths of a box of volume 2 times 3 times 4, that is 24 cubic metres. The tetrahedron occupies one sixth of that box, since it is a pyramid with a right-angled triangular base of area one sixth of the box's base and the same height as the box, and a pyramid is a third of its prism. The volume is therefore 4 cubic metres, and the constant of a sixth is the specific correction a tetrahedron needs.
questions.hint: Treat it as a pyramid: one third of the prism built on its own triangular base.

questions.learningObjective: find the volume left between a cone and its cylinder
questions.stem: A cone with a base of radius 5 centimetres and a perpendicular height of 12 centimetres sits inside a cylinder with exactly the same base and the same height, sharing both circular faces. options.text: 628.32, since the cylinder holds two lots of pi r squared h
314.16, which is the cone's own volume and not the leftover space
options.misconception: reports the cone that was taken away rather than the space that is left

options.text: 942.48, which allows for the base discs at both ends as well
options.misconception: adds on the flat circular faces as though they were part of the volume

options.text: 471.24, which halves the cylinder before taking anything out
options.misconception: halves the cylinder first, which no part of the solid justifies

The empty space is what remains, so it is two thirds of the cylinder, giving 628.32 cubic centimetres. The shared circular faces are surfaces with no thickness, so they contribute nothing to either volume, and the one third factor is the single fact that separates a cone from its cylinder.

Attach the unit, because a magnitude of a cross product is an area

Measure that normal list, which is the area of the box's base face
Multiply the parts of the third list by the parts of the normal one
Add those products and take the size of the total for the volume

Measure the height straight off the base, not along a sloping side edge

Take a third of that result, since a pyramid fills a third of its prism

Measure each of the two direction lists, so the divisor can be formed
Measure the distance between two points on the lines, which sets the angle

options.text: Divide the first result by the product of the two measured lengths

questions.explanation: The angle is recovered from a cosine, and a cosine is a dot product divided by the product of the two magnitudes, so the dot product and the two magnitudes are all genuinely required. The final division is what turns a raw product into a ratio between minus one and one, and only after it does the angle itself appear. A distance between points is not part of the calculation at all, since an angle depends on directions and directions are scale-free, so any distance can be changed by moving the points along their lines.

questions.topic: What must be checked before two lines in space are parallel

options.text: Compare the two direction lists for a common constant multiple
Confirm the two lines share no point, since a meeting pair is not parallel
Confirm the two lines lie at right angles, since that also separates them
options.misconception: treats perpendicular lines as if they were parallel and so close to one another

options.text: Confirm the two lines are the same distance from the origin throughout

questions.explanation: Parallel lines in space are parallel exactly when one direction list is a constant multiple of the other, which is the substantive test and has to be done on the directions rather than on any single pair of points. A shared point then rules out the one case that survives, since two coincident lines have proportional directions as well but meet everywhere. A constant distance from the origin is a further quick check on the placement, while a right angle between the lines is no evidence at all, since perpendicular lines are as far from parallel as skew ones are.
questions.hint: Proportional directions are the test; a shared point is what must then be excluded.

Divide the points by three, since a plane is the average of its points

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof that a cross product measures parallelogram area
questions.learningObjective: prove the area interpretation of a cross product's magnitude
questions.stem: Write a short proof that the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors with lengths a and b meeting at an angle t equals the area of the parallelogram built on those two sides.

answer.exemplar: Let u and v be the two vectors, with |u| = a, |v| = b, and let t be the angle between them. Take the base of the parallelogram to be the side of length a, and let h be the perpendicular distance from the far end of the other side to the line of the base. Dropping a perpendicular from the far corner of that side produces a right triangle whose hypotenuse is b and whose angle at the base is t, so h = b sin t. The area of the parallelogram is base times height, that is a times h, which is a b sin t. By the defining property of the cross product, |u by v| = |u| |v| sin t = a b sin t. The two expressions are identical, so the magnitude of the cross product is exactly the area of the parallelogram. Since a diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two congruent triangles, the area of the triangle on the same two sides is |u by v| / 2. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: The proof turns on writing the parallelogram's area in a way that exposes the sine, and the perpendicular height is where the sine appears. Once that is done the cross product's own defining formula matches term for term, so nothing further needs to be shown. The triangle result follows immediately because the diagonal bisects the area.
questions.hint: Write the parallelogram's area as base times perpendicular height, and find that height from a right triangle.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof that a parallel cross-section is similar to the base
questions.learningObjective: prove that a plane cut parallel to a base is similar to it
questions.stem: Write a short proof that a plane cutting a pyramid parallel to its base produces a cross-section similar to the base, and state the ratio that fixes the scale of that similarity.

answer.exemplar: Let V be the apex of the pyramid, let the base be the triangle ABC, and let the cutting plane meet the edges VA, VB and VC at A', B' and C'. Take the plane through V and the centre of the base, so that it cuts the pyramid in a triangle with apex V and base running along a line of the base, and it cuts the cutting plane in a parallel line since the two planes are parallel. Call the distances from V to the base line and to the cutting line h and h'. The small triangle at V with base on the cutting line and the whole triangle at V with base on the base line share the angle at V, and their other angles are equal because their two base lines are parallel, so the two triangles are similar by two equal angles. In a similar triangle the ratio of the bases equals the ratio of the altitudes, so BC over B'C' equals h over h', and the scaling factor of the cross-section is h' over h. Applying the same argument in every vertical plane through the apex shows that every side of the cross-section is scaled by that one factor, so A'B'C' is similar to ABC. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: The whole proof lives in a single vertical cross-section, where a parallel hypothesis turns into a pair of parallel lines and therefore into equal angles. From the two-angle criterion the small triangle and the whole triangle are similar, and in similar triangles the bases scale with the altitudes. Rotating that argument around the apex is what carries the conclusion from one cross-section to the whole cut face.
questions.hint: Cut through the apex, and use the parallel lines to get two equal angles.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Proof that a cross product is perpendicular to both inputs
questions.learningObjective: prove a cross product is orthogonal to each of its two factors
questions.stem: Write a short proof that the cross product of two vectors is at right angles to each of the two vectors it was built from.

answer.exemplar: Let u = (u1, u2, u3), v = (v1, v2, v3), and w = u by v, so that w1 = u2 v3 - u3 v2, w2 = u3 v1 - u1 v3, and w3 = u1 v2 - u2 v1. The dot product of w with u is u1 w1 + u2 w2 + u3 w3, which expands to u1 u2 v3 - u1 u3 v2 + u2 u3 v1 - u2 u1 v3 + u3 u1 v2 - u3 u2 v1. Every term appears once with a plus and once with a minus, since u1 u2 v3 cancels - u2 u1 v3, u1 u3 v2 cancels - u3 u1 v2, and u2 u3 v1 cancels - u3 u2 v1, so the whole expression is zero. Therefore w is at right angles to u. The same expansion with the parts of v instead gives zero as well, so w is at right angles to v too. Since two non-parallel vectors span a plane and w is at right angles to both, w is normal to that plane. Q.E.D.

questions.explanation: Orthogonality is not something extra that has to be assumed about the cross product, it falls out of the cancellation in its own definition. Each surviving term of the dot product appears once with each sign, so the sum vanishes identically, and the same argument works against either input. The result is stronger than a single right angle, because a vector at right angles to two independent vectors is normal to the whole plane they span.
questions.hint: Expand the dot product against each input and collect the surviving terms in pairs.
